Picture a fire alarm installed not after the fire but before the house is built — and, on top of that, everyone agrees in advance: if the sensor shows such-and-such a concentration of smoke, the residents are obliged to leave, not to argue in the smoke about whether it is worth leaving. The trouble is that the alarm is designed, installed, and maintained by the very developer who would much rather not evacuate profitable tenants. This tension — between "tie your own hands in advance" and "but I myself hold the key to the handcuffs" — is the very heart of today's beast.

The Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP) is an attempt to translate anxiety about dangerous AI capabilities into an engineering discipline with one simple grammar: IF — THEN. IF a model reaches a predefined threshold of a dangerous capability on a measurable test, THEN predefined protective measures switch on automatically — up to and including putting training or deployment on pause until the defense catches up with the threat. No "we'll decide later, depending on how things go." The decision is made while heads are cool and no quarterly release is yet on the line.

At Anthropic this grammar takes the form of a ladder of ASL levels — AI Safety Levels, deliberately modeled on the biosafety levels (BSL) under which laboratories work with pathogens. ASL-1 — systems with no meaningful catastrophic risk (a chess engine). ASL-2 — today's large models, which can give out dangerous information but not much better than a search engine. ASL-3 — models that already noticeably raise the ability of, say, a non-expert to assemble a biological or chemical weapon, or that display dangerous autonomy; for them, stronger security measures and protection of the model weights are required. ASL-4 and above — for now hypothetical territory that the policy promises to describe later, before you run into it. The key move: the thresholds are tied not to the calendar or the size of the model but to dangerous capability evaluations — concrete measurements on concrete tasks. As long as the measurement is below the line — we drive on. Crossed the line — stop, switch on the protocol.

Why bind yourself with a promise at all, if you could just "try to be careful"? Because caution doesn't survive competition well. In the AI race every developer knows: if they slow down for checks, a rival will not, and will take the market. This is the classic race to the bottom — everyone floors the gas not because they want to but because they fear falling behind, and in the end they collectively drive faster than is safe for all. The if-then commitment tries to break this logic preemptively: it makes paying the safety tax (the slowdown, the extra spending on checks and defense) a rule, announced publicly and in advance, rather than an act of goodwill. And — ideally — it creates a template that others can adopt, so that "safe" does not mean "loser." Hence the hope for a warning shot: a tripped threshold is not a catastrophe but its shadow, a signal that still leaves time to retreat.

How it came about. The idea crystallized in 2023 at the junction of two organizations, METR and Anthropic. METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research, then a team grown out of ARC Evals led by Beth Barnes) was doing exactly what almost no one had done systematically before: trying to measure what a model is really capable of in terms of dangerous autonomy and replication. Out of this work grew the formulation of the whole class of policies — "responsible scaling policies": the linkage "measured a capability — checked it against a threshold — switched on a predefined measure."

The first company to put this into a public document was Anthropic — its RSP came out in September 2023 and introduced the ASL ladder. Fairly quickly the genre was taken up by competitors, each under its own name: OpenAI in December 2023 published the Preparedness Framework with a "Scorecard" of risk levels by category (cyber, CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear), persuasion, model autonomy). Google DeepMind in May 2024 released the Frontier Safety Framework with the notion of "critical capability levels." Different vocabularies — a common if-then grammar. In October 2024 Anthropic rewrote its policy as version 2.0, making the capability thresholds and the required safeguards more explicit, and in the spring of 2025 it applied the ASL-3 regime in practice for the first time, when it released the top model of the Claude family, Claude Opus 4. The policy had turned from a philosophical declaration into a working rulebook whose trigger had actually fired.

Criticism / arguments against.

First, voluntariness. This is not a law or a contract with sanctions — it is a public promise a company made to itself. There is no external body to enforce it, no penalty for violation beyond the reputational one. The promise holds exactly as long as keeping it is cheaper than breaking it.

Second, and this is the hardest: the thresholds are set by the developer itself. The one who draws the "dangerous" line has a vital interest in their model turning out to be just a bit below it. The line can be drawn a little higher, the test worded a little softer, the "dangerous capability" defined so that you never technically reach it. This is a conflict of interest sewn into the very construction: judge, defendant, and manufacturer of the evidence are one and the same person.

Third, "safety-washing" — the risk that the policy works not as a brake but as a decoration. A handsome document on the website, shown to regulators and journalists, lets a company keep scaling while creating the impression of control where there is little control. Thresholds that never trip are indistinguishable from their absence — but look more respectable.

Fourth, commitments can be weakened retroactively. Since the company writes the policy, the company also rewrites it. Having discovered that approaching a threshold threatens to halt an expensive release, the company can, just before the release, "refine" the definitions, soften the requirements, or shift the line. Formally the policy is observed — it was simply quietly edited to fit the result. Observers have more than once pointed out that the versions of these documents evolve, and not always toward greater strictness.

And the general, most uncomfortable question: the measurements are immature. We are still poor at reliably measuring a "dangerous capability" — a model can hide skills on tests, or suddenly acquire them from a little fine-tuning after the check. A threshold whose crossing cannot be reliably detected is a door without a lock, to which a "locked" sign has been attached.

What to do about it / where it leads. RSPs are not a solution but scaffolding. Their value is not that they have already stopped anyone, but that they forced the industry, for the first time, to say aloud the concrete conditions for stopping — and thereby gave everyone else a point of leverage for their demands. When a threshold is named publicly, it is easier to catch whoever shifts it red-handed.

First — externalize the check: the thresholds and tests should be set and validated by independent parties (METR, state AI safety institutes, external auditors), not only by the developer itself. The judge cannot be the defendant. Second — back the voluntary commitment with law, so that violating "if — then" carries a cost beyond reputational risk. Third, and technically key — hitch the thresholds to compute governance: training compute can be measured, registered, and controlled from outside far better than a vague "capability," and so it is compute that can become the physical lever turning a promise into an enforceable rule.

Either "if — then" matures into a common, externally verifiable norm that is mandatory by law — and then the warning shot really will sound in time, before the live one. Or it remains a handsome promise, rewritten for each release — and then we will learn only after the fact that the threshold was not where it should have been. This beast is useful, but only half-tamed: it shows where the dangerous line runs, but for now it itself holds the chalk with which the line is drawn.
